q.t: What is sound?
o: A vibration that travels through the air
q.e: A shaking string pushes the air, the air pushes your eardrum, and you hear it.

q.t: What does pitch mean?
o: How high or low a note sounds
q.e: Pitch is high or low. Loud or soft is a different thing (loudness).

q.t: Which string sounds higher?
q.e: A thin, light string springs back faster, so it shakes more times per second and sounds higher.

q.t: Pressing a string down at a fret makes the shaking part of the string…
o: shorter, so the note goes up
longer, so the note goes down
thicker, so the note goes down
louder, but the note stays the same
q.e: The fret stops the string, so only the part between the fret and the bridge shakes. Shorter → higher.

q.t: Frequency is measured in…
q.e: 1 hertz = one shake per second.

q.t: You pluck a string much harder. What happens?
q.e: Plucking harder makes the string swing wider (louder), but it swings at the same speed (same pitch).

q.t: What do you turn to tune a string?
q.e: The peg changes how tight the string is, and tighter means higher.

q.t: Which fret is exactly halfway along the string?
q.e: Fret 12 (the double dot) is the halfway point, which gives the octave.

q.t: What turns the string's shaking into an electric signal on an electric guitar?
q.e: Pickups are magnets wrapped in wire. The steel string moving over them makes a small electric signal.

q.t: What should you do before plugging the cable into the amp?
o: Turn the amp volume to full
q.e: Plugging in makes a loud pop. With the volume down, it can't hurt your ears or the speaker.

q.t: Which change makes a string sound lower?
q.e: A looser string springs back more slowly, so it shakes fewer times per second — lower pitch.

q.t: The open A string shakes about 110 times a second. What is its frequency?
q.e: Shakes per second = hertz, so 110 shakes a second is 110 Hz.

q.t: Why are electric guitar strings made of steel?
o: The magnetic pickups only notice metal
Steel strings never go out of tune
Steel strings are always louder unplugged
Nylon is too thick for frets
q.e: A magnet only senses metal moving near it. A nylon string would make no signal.

q.t: Why is an electric guitar quiet when it is not plugged in?
o: Its solid body does not boom like a hollow box
The pickups soak up the sound
q.e: An acoustic's hollow body makes the sound louder. The electric's solid body doesn't, so it needs an amp.

q.t: Which pickup gives a warm, round sound?
o: Neither — only the amp changes tone
q.e: The neck pickup is warm and round; the bridge pickup is bright and sharp.

q.t: What does turning the gain up on the amp do?
q.e: Low gain = clean. High gain = distorted rock sound.

q.t: You stop a ringing string with your hand. Why does the sound stop?
o: The string can no longer shake
Your hand soaks up the electricity
The string goes out of tune
q.e: No shaking means no push on the air, so no sound.

q.t: A ruler hangs off a desk. Which way does it wobble fastest when flicked?
o: With only a short piece hanging off
With a long piece hanging off
It wobbles the same either way
When it is not touching the desk
q.e: A short piece springs back faster — just like a short (fretted) string sounds higher.

q.t: A note at the 12th fret sounds like the open string, but…
q.e: Halving the length doubles the shakes per second — the same note, an octave higher.

q.t: Which is the best amp sound for a beginner practising?
o: Loud, with the tone knob at zero
q.e: A clean sound lets you hear every mistake and every accidental string, so you can fix them.

q.t: The open A string is 110 Hz. What is the A at the 12th fret?
q.e: Fret 12 is halfway, and half the length doubles the frequency: 110 × 2 = 220 Hz.

q.t: The low E string is about 82 Hz. Roughly what is the E an octave higher?
q.e: One octave up = twice the frequency: 82 × 2 = 164 Hz.

q.t: Two notes are an octave apart. One is 196 Hz. The lower one is…
q.e: The lower note of an octave shakes half as fast: 196 ÷ 2 = 98 Hz.

q.t: Why do two notes an octave apart get the same letter name?
o: Their shakes line up every second swing
They are both played on the same string
They come from the same pickup
q.e: One shakes exactly twice as fast, so the shakes match up very often. Our ears hear them as the same note, higher and lower.

q.t: Loudness depends on how ___ the string swings; pitch depends on how ___ it swings.
q.e: A wider swing pushes more air (louder). A faster swing makes more shakes per second (higher).

q.t: All six strings are the same length. Why do they sound different notes?
o: Some are plugged in, some are not
q.e: Thinner and tighter strings shake faster. The strings are made different thicknesses and tuned to different tightnesses.

q.t: A string sounds too low on the tuner. What should you do?
q.e: Too low (flat) means it is shaking too slowly. Tightening makes it shake faster.

q.t: A guitar and a piano play the same A. Why do they still sound different?
q.e: Both shake at the same main frequency, but each adds its own mix of quieter, higher overtones — its tone colour.

q.t: What does the tone knob do when you turn it down?
o: Makes the sound softer and warmer
q.e: Turning tone down cuts the bright, sharp part of the sound, so it sounds warmer.

q.t: Put the path of the sound in order.
q.e: The string shakes over the pickup, the cable carries the signal, the amp makes it bigger, and the speaker shakes the air.

q.t: A note is 440 Hz. What is the note two octaves higher?
q.e: Each octave doubles the frequency: 440 × 2 = 880, × 2 again = 1760 Hz.

q.t: A note is 330 Hz. What is the note one octave lower?
q.e: One octave down = half the frequency: 330 ÷ 2 = 165 Hz.

q.t: If you halve the shaking length of a string, its frequency…
q.e: Half the length springs back twice as fast, so twice the shakes per second — one octave up.

q.t: A string is in tune. You press fret 12 and the note is a little higher than an exact octave. What does this tell you?
o: Something needs adjusting, as fret 12 should give an exact octave
That is normal — fret 12 is never an octave
The string is too thin to play
The tone knob is turned too far
q.e: Fret 12 is the halfway point, so it should give exactly twice the open frequency. If not, the guitar's setup needs adjusting (a shop can fix this).

q.t: You tune past the note and it is now too high. What is the best way to finish?
o: Go below the note, then tune up to it
Loosen it until it reaches the note
q.e: Finishing by tightening pulls the string snug around the peg so it stays in tune. Finishing by loosening lets it slip.

q.t: Why does distortion make beginner mistakes harder to hear?
o: It makes every sound big, even accidental ones
It turns the guitar off for wrong notes
It changes all notes to one pitch
It only works on the neck pickup
q.e: Distortion squashes loud and soft together and makes everything sustain, so buzzes and stray strings blur in.

q.t: Which change would not raise the pitch of a string?
q.e: Plucking harder only makes it louder (wider swing), not faster.

q.t: A string shakes 220 times in one second. How many times does it shake in half a second?
q.e: Half the time, half the shakes: 220 ÷ 2 = 110.

q.t: Two strings: one shakes 300 times a second, the other 150. Which is true?
o: They are an octave apart; 300 is higher
They are an octave apart; 150 is higher
They are the same note and pitch
q.e: 300 is exactly 2 × 150, so they are an octave apart. More shakes per second = higher.

q.t: Why must you finger a string to change notes on a guitar, but not on a piano?
o: A guitar string changes length; each piano key has its own string
Piano strings are made of nylon
Guitar strings are all the same thickness
q.e: A piano has a separate string for every note. A guitar has six strings, so you shorten them with frets to get the other notes.
